TESTIMONY OF THE MAINE MEDICAL ASSOCIATION, THE MAINE OSTEOPATHIC ASSOCIATION, AND THE MAINE CHAPTER, AMERICAN ACADEMY OF PEDIATRICS
In Opposition to
LD 410 An Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-not-resuscitate Order for a Minor
Ioint Standing Committee on Judiciary
Room 438, State House, Augusta, Maine
Tuesday, March 4, 2025
Good Afternoon, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Iudiciary. My name is Anne Sedlack, and I am the Director of Advocacy at the Maine Medical Association. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to LD. 410 An
Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-not-resuscitate Order for a Minor
The Maine Medical Association (MMA) is a professional organization representing more than 4,000 physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine. MMA's mission is to support Maine physicians, advance the quality of medicine in Maine, and promote the health of all Maine people. The Maine Osteopathic Association (MOA) is a professional organization representing more than 1,200 osteopathic physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine whose mission is to serve the Osteopathic profession of the State of Maine through a coordinated effort of professional education, advocacy, and member
services in order to ensure the availability of quality osteopathic health care to the people
of this State. The Maine Chapter, AAP is a membership organization of 220 pediatricians and subspecialists who are dedicated to fulfilling the Chapter's mission: to improve the
lives of children and adolescents in Maine.
We have joined to advocate with one voice. We have all determined that it is important to
testify in opposition to LD 410.
Pediatric end-of-life care is nuanced and deeply personal. In some tragic cases, life-sustaining treatment may prolong suffering without the possibility of recovery. Physicians, guided by rigorous ethical principles, work in partnership with families and the rest of the medical team to determine when continued intervention is no longer in a child's best interest. This bill imposes a rigid framework that could force physicians to administer futile and painful treatments against medical recommendations.
1

Existing laws and hospital policies already provide robust safeguards to ensure that parents are involved in decisions regarding their child's care. Ethics committees, second
opinions, and legal avenues exist to mediate disputes when theyl arise. This bill, although
well-intentioned, is unnecessary and disruptive to these well-established processes. Unless there is a compelling reason to change long-time established and comprehensive
Maine statutes concerning the medical treatment of minors, we urge the committee to vote
Ought Not to Pass. Thank you for considering the thoughts of Maine's physicians and public health community about LD 410.
Best,
Anne Sedlack

Re: LD 410 -An Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-not-resuscitate Order for a Minor
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition of LD 410.
This bill would establish a statutory prohibition on health care providers withholding lifesustaining care or complying with DNRs without the written consent of a parent or legal guardian for the minor. The bill would also prohibit providers from hindering the transfer of a child to another provider for care and would implement a statutory presumption that continuation of life is in a minor's best interest. The language of LD 410 would require that a parent or legal guardian's authority in these matters does not end. The bill would prohibit compliance with the court order to withdraw life-sustaining care when a parent objects to that court order unless there is "destruction of the circulatory and respiratory systems and the entire brain of the minor."
OCFS opposes this bill because as written, it directly conflicts with the existing statute around DNRs in the Child and Family Services and Child Protection Act. 22 MRSA �4037(2) provides a process for withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining medical treatment for children in the care and custody of the Department. OCFS has an established process for these instances that allows for the parents to provide input when their rights have not been terminated. OCFS has concern about the portion of this law that would allow parents to maintain authority over DNRs and withdrawal of care even if parental rights and responsibilities have been terminated.
This proposal would be particularly problematic in situations where a parent or legal guardian is accused of causing injuries to the child as it would set up a situation where the parent or legal guardian may be making a decision about a DNR and/or withholding life-sustaining measures based on their own best interests and not that of the child. The bill also does not appear to address situations where two parents or legal guardians do not agree on the appropriate course of action for their shared child.
OCFS believes sufficient protections already exist to ensure the rights of parents in making medical decisions for their child, and that 22 MRSA �4037(2) is appropriately utilized in these difficult and unfortunate circumstances when necessary. 4037 ensures that parents whose rights have not been terminated are consulted in these decisions. When the parent does not consent,

4037 also provides authority to the District Court to consider both whether the parent is unfit and whether the withdrawing of life-sustaining treatment is in the best interests of the child.
OCFS encourages you to vote ought not to pass on LD 410 to continue the appropriate balance of the rights of parents and best interest of children.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Bobbi Johnson, LMSW Director Office of Child and Family Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services

184873:
ll; MaineHealth
Testimony of Dr. Allison Caldwell, MaineHealth
In Opposition to LD 410, "An Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-Sustaining Measures for a Minor or
to Comply with a Do-Not-Resuscitate Order for a Minor" March 4, 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Commit-
tee on Judiciary, my name is Dr. Allison Caldwell, Pediatric Palliative Care Physician, and Chief of the Division of Pediatric Palliative Care at Maine Medical Center. I am present today to testify in opposition to LD 410, "An Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-Sustaining
Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-Not-Resuscitate Order for a Minor."
I currently live in Brunswick, Maine, and have lived and practiced medicine in Maine for the
past eight years, where I am also raising my young family. I trained in Pediatrics at Brown University Pediatrics Residency and completed my Pediatric Palliative fellowship training at the University of Tennessee and St. Jude Chi1dren's Research Hospital. In addition to my medical
training, I have a Master's Degree in Medical Ethics.
While my medical practice is geographically located in Southern Maine, my team is the only
Pediatric Palliative Care team in the state of Maine, and we care for children and their families
throughout the entire state. The practice of pediatric palliative care is centered in upholding and uplifting the voices and the quality of life of children and their families as they navigate serious,
complex, and life changing medical conditions. A major part of our job is ensuring that a child
and family has the expert medical information and the support and communication from their medical team that they need to create a medical care plan that matches their hopes, goals, and values. This often includes closely supporting a child and family as they enter into the advanced or late stages of a pediatric illness, and as a family navigates end of life decision making and care
for their child. In this context, a parent or primary guardian may be facing incredibly sensitive,
and truly unimaginable decisions regarding the benefits and risks of specific life-sustaining medical interventions for their child, including, but not limited to, decision making about cardiopul-
monaiy resuscitation, or a "Do Not Resuscitate" order.
With these families of Maine in mind today, I would like to highlight four key points relevant to
LD 410:
1. It is already an established standard of medical-ethical practice, and established law in Maine that parents/guardians must provide consent to withhold life-sustaining measures for a minor, including any change in resuscitation status.
As a physician practicing in pediatric palliative care for nearly a decade, I have directly cared for most of the pediatric patients within the MaineHealth system whose families are navigating the
benefits and risks of life sustaining medical interventions for their child. These decisions are guided by parental autonomy, the best interests of the child, and our responsibility to protect a child from harm. These decisions are always determined with parental/ guardian consent follow-
ing many detailed, comprehensive, and compassionate team discussions with parents/guardians.

Decisions regarding life-sustaining medical interventions are firmly rooted in the goals, values, and beliefs of an individual family, and are approached as such by the pediatric medical team.
The families impacted by this bill are families who have, for example, supported their child through years of intensive cancer treatment, through innumerable ICU hospitalizations with their child with a rare and progressive genetic or neurologic condition; they are families who provide remarkable around-the-clock care at home to their child with chronic severe lung or heart disease, or families whose previously healthy child has experienced a sudden and devastating trau-
matic injury or overwhelming and catastrophic infection. These are parents/guardians with expe-
riences that deeply inform the loving health care decisions they make for their child - medical decisions that for this reason no two families would navigate in the exact same way. Therefore, decisions regarding life-sustaining interventions are always derived based on the most expert medi-
cal information and recommendations of a care team along with the goals, beliefs, and values of the parent/guardian and child. This is the standard of medical practice, and I Want to emphasize that MaineHealth is unaware of any issues that have arisen at any MaineHealth hospital or other care setting involving the withholding of treatment for minors without the knowledge and consent of a parent or guardian. Additionally, parental decision-making rights and parental auton-
omy is already codified and clearly protected in the standards of medical care, professional and
ethical standards of the practice of pediatrics, and in our Maine Statute: Title 22, Chapter 260,
stating "a surrogate may not withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment or deny surgery, pro-
cedures or other interventions that are lifesaving and medically necessary."
2. This bill places a new and impactful burden on a parent/guardian navigating critical and
sensitive medical decision making.
LD 410 would place a significant burden on a parent/guardian at a time in which they are navi-
gating a critical health decision for their child. In the hospital setting, parental/guardian verbal consent is already required to establish care plans pertaining to withholding life sustaining interventions, including resuscitation or code status. This plan is explicitly and clearly established with the parent/guardian and is then documented in writing in multiple locations and by multiple medical providers, including within a patient's medical orders and electronic medical record, which is accessible and transparent for parents/guardians.
The requirements of this bill would go further to require a parent/guardian to provide written consent to either establish or revoke a plan pertaining to life-sustaining medical interventions and resuscitation status. These are the hardest decisions a parent/guardian ever has to make, made from a deep place of love and intense protection for their child when an illness can no longer be reversed, and their goals are centered on their child's comfort. To ask a parent in real-time to then put these decisions into writing creates a high degree of emotional and psychological burden, risk of trauma, and complicated grief. The requirement of written consent and written revocation also risks delaying the provision of care to the child, whether life-sustaining or intensive
comfort-based care.
Of additional concern, the "Failure to Contact," section places further restrictions on parental
rights and on the rights of the child and risks the immediate health and Well-being of the child. In
the event that a parent!guardian were unable to reached in the setting of pediatric illness, DHHS

would be immediately involved in order to identify a guardian for the child. Even in this scenario, the health care team would not make a unilateral health care decision for a pediatric pa-
tient, other than for critical life-saving interventions.
3. LD 410 does not give weight to the complex clinical considerations required to determine
the risks and benefits and safest timeframe within which to pursue interventions including, but not limited to, placement of tracheostomy and gastrostomy tubes, and the initiation of physical transfer and transport to a different medical institution when a pediatric patient is
experiencing critical illness.
In reviewing considerations presented in LD 410 regarding timing of medical procedures, includ-
ing tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placement, as well as transfer to a different health care institution, it's important to note that these are nuanced clinical decisions, requiring a complex
analysis of benefits and risks for an individual child, and are always made with the parent/guardian's input. There are clinical situations in which a patient may be extremely critically ill and un-
stable, and major surgical interventions, transport to an OR setting, and/or long-distance
transport to another health care institution may be extremely high risk and life-threatening. Proceeding with these types of interventions would never be hindered when determined to be medi-
cally appropriate, in line with parent/guardian's goals of care, and safe for the pediatric patient. Furthermore, transfer to a different medical institution would never be delayed or hindered by the placement of a tracheotomy or gastrostomy tube - transfer can occur without either of these long-term interventions, and pediatric patients are frequently transferred supported with the use of equivalent levels of support (utilizing endotracheal tubes, mechanical ventilation, and naso- or orogastric feeding tubes).
4. This bill would serve to contradict and create confusion in the well-established Maine law on the determination of death.
Finally, Sections 6 and 7 of this legislation serve to directly contradict Maine's already clearly established statute regarding the determination of death, which clearly defines and, importantly, separates: "irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory functions" and "irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brain stem" (Title 22, Chapter 706). This would result in significant confusion medically and legally throughout our state.
I would also note that the 130*" Legislature rejected similar legislation, and I would urge this Legislature to reject it once again. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in opposition to this legislation. I would be happy to answer questions.

184870:
MAINE FAMILY LAW ADVISORY COMMISSION

Report to Maine Legislature Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary
On LD 410 "An Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or
to Comply with a Do-not-resuscitate Order for a Minor."
1

Introduction

The Maine Family Law Advisory Commission hereby reports to the Maine Legislature,
Joint "Standing Committee on Judiciary on LD 410, "An Act to Require Parental Consent to
Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-not-resuscitate Order for a Minor." This bill ainils to prohibit health care practitioners, health care providers and facilities such as nursing homes, hospitals and children's homes from withholding life-sustaining measures
or instituting a do-not-resuscitate order for an unemancipated minor without the written consent of a parent or legal guardian of the minor. Health care practitioners, health care providers and
facilities may not hinder a parent or legal guardian of a minor to seek another medical opinion or
transfer the minor to another health care provider or facility and are required to continue providing life-sustaining measures until the transfer, continue to allow access to the minor and the minor's medical records and inform the parent or legal guardian of any policies regarding resuscitation, life-sustaining measures or measures considered nonbeneficial, ineffective, futile or inappropriate for patients or residents. The bill provides that there is a presumption that the continuation of life is in a minor's best interest and that the parental or legal guardian authority does not end and the authority of a court to order the withdrawal of life-sustaining measures from a minor does not take precedence over the objections of a parent or legal guardian of the minor unless there is destruction of the circulatory and respiratory systems and the entire brain of the minor.

Pursuant to 19-A MRS � 354(2) and in furtherance of its statutory mandate to examine,

evaluate, and recommend to the Legislature changes in family law that it considers advisable,

FLAC has reviewed and considered the proposed legislation. For the reasons set out below,

FLAC's position on LD 492 is as follows:

,

Discussion
'
Although there are only a small number of cases this type of legislation would impact, the
cases that are impacted are typically tragedies for a family. Notwithstanding obvious technical issues with the bill, the bill would influence, whether intended to or not, an extremely complex
area of the law and in many instances a family with very complex family dynamics. The laws affected are not only complex, but also have many judicial bypass laws including the capacity for
informed consent that would be impacted by this legislation. Ultimately, this bill could impact decision making involving organ transplants, blood transfusions, and life-threatening medical
procedures. Before enacting this bill or considering its subject matter further, FLAC recommends
that the legislature conduct research to determine how many statutes would be affected and how many may need amendments to resolve conflicts arising from its passage. Additionally, the
potential impact of LD 410 on how the District and Probate Courts handle informed consent issues

1

could be significant and should be thoroughly examined. FLAC can aid should the Committee

choose to consider this bill further.

.

In summary, the impact of this bill may potentially be significant, wide ranging, and could
result in costly litigation in some instances.

Conclusion
For all these reasons, FLAC does not support LD 410.

Parental involvement is fundamental in the healthcare decisions of minors. LD 410 reinforces this principle by: � Requiring Written Consent: Healthcare providers must obtain written consent from a parent or legal guardian before withholding life-sustaining measures or implementing a DNR order for a minor. � Ensuring Transparency: The bill mandates that healthcare practitioners disclose any policies regarding resuscitation and life-sustaining measures upon request, fostering trust and clear communication between families and medical professionals.
States across the nation have recognized the importance of safeguarding parental rights in medical decisions for minors. For instance:
� Kansas: Enacted Simon's Law to ensure parents are informed and provide consent before a DNR order is placed on a minor's medical chart.
� Missouri: Passed legislation requiring parental notification and consent for DNR orders for minors. � Idaho: Implemented laws to protect parental rights in decisions about life-sustaining treatment for
minors.
LD 410 is a vital piece of legislation that upholds the rights of parents to be fully informed and to consent to significant medical decisions affecting their children. By enacting this bill, Maine will join other states in affirming the essential role of parents in the healthcare of their minor children, ensuring that such critical decisions are made collaboratively and transparently.
I urge the Judiciary Committee to support LD 410. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Nicholas Adolphsen Executive Director

Reagan Paul and I represent House District 37 which includes the towns of Winterport, Prospect, Stockton
Springs, Searsport, and part of Frankfort. I am proud to stand before you today to present my bill LD 410: "An
Act to Require Parental Consent to Withhold Life-sustaining Measures for a Minor or to Comply with a Do-
not-resuscitate Orderfor a Minor. "
There is a Nazi-style eugenics--driven genocide of children, happening in our nation's hospitals, which blatantly disregards your parental right to make critical medical decisions for your child. In most states, it is perfectly legal for a doctor to unilaterally decide that your precious child is not worthy of life preservation, and instruct
medical staff to withhold resuscitative measures, by placing a Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order in your child's
medical chart, without making any effort to obtain your written informed consent.
Typically, these are children that the medical establishment believe to be intellectually disabled, due to their apparent or suspected inability to communicate sufficiently. These could be infants diagnosed with syndromes associated with diminished or delayed neurological functions; children deprived of oxygen during birth, or as
the result of drowning or other unfortunate situations; teenagers who sustained traumatic brain injuries in a high impact incident; or, minors whose brain was compromised by a virus, bacteria, fever, cancer, seizure, or toxic
substance (ingested or injected). Regardless of the situation or cause, doctor's are acting within the authority of their facility's futilig policy to forgo cardiopulmonary resuscitative (CPR) measures; and, even delay,
withhold, or deny the administration of life-sustaining nutrition, hydration, and oxygen, to children they deem
incompatible with life. There is a clear difference between the futility of a treatment and the futility of
someone's life. Too often, providers use the term "futile" in describing someone's quality of life. To say that an individual's life is "futile" because it may appear short, difficult, or full of pain introduces a subjective value judgement that no one but the parent's may appropriately or ethically determine. In addition, healthcare
providers and medical institutions could gain significant legal protection if they are no longer liable for these challenging "life and death" decisions for minor children.

final authority over critical medical decisions impacting the sustained life of your child! These are difficult and

complex decisions, with grave ramifications resting squarely on the shoulders of parents. Thus, your right to choose what is best for your child should be held in the highest regard!
My bill, which is known throughout the country as Simon's Law, is named in honor of a precious little boy
named Simon Crosier, whose parents you will hear from shortly. I will let them tell you his story. The primary
objective of my bill is to restore parental rights in decisions relating to life-sustaining care (based on the
presumption that the continuation of life is in the minor's best interest), by making it illegal for doctors to
institute DNRs without the written permission of parents. This includes a requirement to aid in the smooth and
speedy access of alternative opinions; and, to cooperatively facilitate a seamless life-sustaining transfer to a different facility. Furthermore, transparency is required on any existing policies involving resuscitation or lifesustaining measures.
In conclusion, We must stand together to protect the most fundamental right a parent has--the right to decide what is best for their child, especially when it comes to matters of life and death. No medical professional, no
matter their title or expertise, should ever have the authority to override the voice of a parent in the most critical
moments of their child's life. With Simon's Law, we aim to restore this essential right, ensuring that no child is
denied the chance at life based on subjective judgments or bureaucratic policies. This is not just a fight for Simon--it is a fight for all our children, for the future of parental rights, and for the preservation of life itself.
Together, We can make sure that every child, no matter their condition, receives the care and respect they
deserve.
Sincerely,
